description:
Heyaa moon-goers! 

We're The Voyagers! Wanna land on the cheese wheel dangling above our heads? Wanna make sure you or your best robot friends land safe and sound? Well our website is just for you! 

Powered by sleep deprived coders and hours of heads banging against walls, we made Astropulse! 

Our team LOVES coding and tinkering with all kinds of stuff, hardware, software, app, websites. You name it, we make it! This year, we're dipping our feet into the fantasic realm of 3D! We learnt 3D modeling, simulations, and even data analysis and interpretation whist having lots of fun! 

If you are scientists or nerds who love the moon, come and take a look at our website, we are sure you'll absolutely love it. See you there! ❤️
summary: Astropulse is an interactive webapp that enables researchers and the public to evaluate and compare candidate landing sites side-by-side across customizable dates and times. By selecting a lunar coordinate, users can visualize surface topography alongside the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon. For every scenario, the platform calculates critical feasibility metrics—including solar illumination duration, Sun elevation angles, time until sunset, local surface temperatures, Earth visibility windows, signal delay, time until Earthset, solar irradiance and water ice stability. Ultimately, by demonstrating how minor shifts in landing coordinates or mission timing dramatically impact power, thermal survival, and communications, the application demystifies the complex engineering behind lunar exploration.
details:
Astropulse is a full-stack web application built with Python Flask on the backend and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on the frontend, developed in Visual Studio Code. It is deployed on Vercel to deliver a fast, scalable, and responsive user experience. Let's explore Astropulse page by page.

Our Github page: https://github.com/Victorhii/astropulse

1. Dashboard

Astropulse Dashboard is the home page of the Astropulse web app. It shows a live UTC clock, the current lunar day in its 29.5-day cycle, and a real-time 3D Moon whose lighting matches the Sun’s current position. A collapsible sidebar provides navigation to the other sections of the app.

On load, a Flask endpoint fetches the current time from timeapi.io, and the page uses that offset to keep the clock and calculations synced to UTC. The lunar day is calculated from the time elapsed since a known new moon, divided by the synodic month of 29.53 days. The Moon itself is a sphere rendered with Three.js, wrapped in an 8K texture from Solar System Scope that Flask serves. Its sunlight direction and tilt are computed from orbital formulas for the Sun and Moon, so the phase and libration match the synced date.

2. Comparison

(a) Query Page

The query page sets up the comparison by letting the user configure four target sites, each with a lunar coordinate, a UTC date and time, and a shared temperature range. Coordinates can be picked from a 3D Moon globe, a searchable catalogue of past and planned missions, or entered manually, so both expert and general users can start from a familiar entry point.

(b) Result Page

The results page is the main comparison and has three parts. A feasibility podium ranks the four sites by weighted score, giving an immediate answer. The sites are evaluated with eight criteria: earth elevation angle, earth event, solar elevation angle, solar event, solar irradiance, lunar diurnal temperature range and terrain slope angle. Eight criteria cards then show each site’s value on a scaled bar, crown the best performer, and explain why each metric matters. These cards reveal the trade-offs that a single percentage hides. This page also features a colourful PDF export for record-keeping.

The data comes from two Python modules - app.py caches the 8K lunar texture and the LOLA-based elevation, slope, and ice maps, and fetches the current UTC time. lunar_probe.py uses NASA SPICE ephemeris kernels to compute Sun and Earth positions and horizon events, reads LOLA terrain data in small patches via HTTP Range requests, and estimates surface temperature with a thermal model. The ice index is a thermal proxy and does not yet account for shadowed craters.

3. Simulation

(a) Selection Page

The selection page is an interactive 3D Moon globe that helps users choose a landing site. Users can rotate it and switch one surface layer at a time: elevation, slope angle, or water ice stability. This visual step makes terrain and ice patterns visible before any numbers are compared, so users can pick promising regions quickly. Coordinates can also be chosen from past missions or entered manually, and the same selection flows into the simulation.

(b) Main Simulation Page

The main simulation places the user at a 1.7 m eye height on realistic lunar topography, with the real Sun and Earth positioned by NASA SPICE ephemerides. A 360-degree horizon, computed from LOLA elevation data, shows whether terrain blocks either body, and a relay alert appears when Earth is hidden. A telemetry panel reports the selected coordinate and UTC time, along with Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation, sightlines, Earth phase, sun elevation angle, and time before sunset or Earthset. This view matters because it shows what a crew member or rover operator would actually see, which is the clearest way to judge whether a site is operationally viable.

Timeline mode extends the analysis across a user-defined range of up to 399 days. A bottom time bar overlays sunlight and Direct-to-Earth windows on a scrubber, so users can jump to the exact moment they intend to land or communicate. This makes the timing trade-offs that drive mission scheduling visible at a glance.

When the user confirms a site and datetime, the browser sends a GET request to /api/lunar-sim-data, triggering build_simulation_payload() in lunar_sim_service.py. Two workstreams run in parallel: a thread pool fetches LOLA DEM patches via HTTP Range headers — a 14 km inner patch for the terrain mesh and a 42 km outer patch for the horizon profile — reading only the bytes needed rather than the full 2 GB raster. All SPICE calls run under a mutex lock, computing Sun and Earth topocentric positions, angular sizes, and illumination vectors in the Moon's local East-North-Up frame, alongside surface temperature, water ice stability, slope, and the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, and Earthset events.

The outer patch is passed through _compute_horizon_profile(), which bins terrain points into 360 azimuth slots and takes the maximum elevation per slot. The server packs this horizon array alongside both elevation grids as Base64 Float32 binary into one JSON payload. The browser decodes the grids into Three.js displacement meshes, while a horizon texture fed into the fragment shader determines in real time whether the Sun or Earth is terrain-occluded. The Earth renders as a procedurally shaded disc using SPICE-derived terminator and rotation vectors; the Sun as a physically sized disc with a corona. Timeline mode samples the same endpoint across a user-defined date range, plots sunlight and Direct-to-Earth windows as coloured bands on the scrubber, and reloads the full simulation at any selected moment.

4. Knowledge

The knowledge page is an educational hub that explains why the Moon is such a demanding environment for missions. It covers six core challenges: two-week days and nights, extreme temperature swings, Earth signal blackouts, long polar shadows, the water-ice paradox, and steep slopes with sharp dust. A scenario-based sensitivity explorer then lets visitors switch between a latitude shift, a 5 km micro-shift, and a 7-day launch delay to see how small changes in location or timing reshape power, temperature, and communication conditions. A closing section on core trade-offs, such as solar power versus water-ice access, shows that no lunar site scores perfectly on every criterion.

The page matters because it turns the technical complexity behind Astropulse into accessible understanding for students, the public, and new team members. The sensitivity explorer is especially valuable because it makes the central lesson of the project tangible: a few kilometres or a single week can change whether a mission succeeds. That insight supports the rest of the platform by explaining why the comparison and simulation tools exist and how to interpret their results.

Overall


Astropulse consolidates SPICE ephemerides, LOLA terrain data, thermal models, and communication windows into one accessible platform, eliminating the need to juggle multiple specialist tools. Mission planners can compare up to four landing sites across eight weighted criteria and export findings as a PDF, while educators and the public gain intuition through the sensitivity explorer and first-person lunar simulation.

The project's intended impact is to bridge the gap between NASA's published technical data and the rapid, agile decisions that real mission development demands. Creatively, it goes beyond the challenge brief by pairing genuine physics — SPICE-driven celestial positions and LOLA terrain fetched via HTTP Range requests — with an immersive WebGL simulation, a layered globe, and plain-language explanations, all deployed on Vercel with no installation required, making it equally useful to a professional planner and a curious student.


USE OF AI


Claude (Anthropic) — backend logic: lunar data fetching, SPICE integration, LOLA terrain pipeline, thermal model, and site scoring engine.

Gemini (Google DeepMind) — frontend: UI layout, simulation WebGL rendering, and timeline mode.
